item.title: Ensuring there is enough to eat. [ dhakatribune ]
item.description:
The latest warnings from the World Bank regarding soaring global commodity prices and worsening food insecurity should serve as a warning for policy-makers in our country.
With global food prices projected to climb 10% this year and another 7% in 2027, driven by compounding geopolitical shocks, energy spikes, and climate anomalies, the external economic environment is turning perilous.
For our nation, where millions are already battered by a prolonged inflation crisis, real-wage squeeze, and a 3.4% GDP growth slowdown that have pushed over 2.1 million new citizens into poverty, we cannot wait until the situation becomes even more precarious.
Food security is not merely an economic metric but the ultimate test of national survival. When global grain supply lines fracture and fertilizer and fuel costs surge, import-dependent economies, which we unfortunately are, face immediate vulnerability.
Yet, while international warnings mount, domestic market syndicates, hoarding rings, and other bad actors continue to artificially inflate essential food prices inside our own borders. This results in bleeding dry a population where nearly half of all households are already taking on high-interest informal debt just to buy daily meals.
Ensuring that every citizen has guaranteed access to affordable food must therefore become the singular, uncompromised focus of the state.
From bolstering national strategic food reserves to diversifying import sources to bypass regional supply disruptions to ruthlessly dismantling domestic syndicates that prey on hungry families, we need an efficient, coordinated, and proactive reaction.
Furthermore, agricultural inputs such as fertilizers, power, and seed support must be secured for farmers to maximize local crop yields and insulate the country from external shocks.
There is nothing more important than ensuring no citizen goes to sleep hungry. We must secure our food supply chains and treat national food security as the absolute, non-negotiable bottom line of survival.

item.title: Beyond academic excellence: How Bangladesh can nurture students with an ethical compass. [ dhakatribune ]
item.description:
Bangladesh is a land of enormous potential where its greatest asset is the intellectual energy, creativity, and ambition of its people, particularly its younger generation.
If we are to transform our country into a prosperous, innovative, and respected nation, we must invest in the quality of our human capital.
But a fundamental question deserves our attention: Are we preparing our young people only to succeed in life, or also to live a life of integrity?
Academic qualifications, professional skills, and technological competence are essential in today's competitive world. Yet these attributes alone cannot guarantee an honest business leader, an accountable public servant, a responsible citizen, or a compassionate human being.
Knowledge gives us the ability to act; an ethical compass helps us decide how and why we should act.
Bangladesh must therefore build an education system that nurtures both intellectual excellence and moral responsibility. Our objective should be to produce not merely successful graduates, but individuals capable of navigating life's moral dilemmas with wisdom, courage, and integrity.
Most of us grow up learning that honesty is a virtue, corruption is wrong, fairness matters, and others deserve respect. Yet real life often presents situations in which doing the right thing is neither easy nor convenient.
A student may witness a classmate cheating in an examination and struggle to decide whether to report it. A young professional may discover that securing a business advantage requires an unofficial payment. A public servant may face pressure to favour a relative over a deserving applicant.
These are not simply questions of knowing right from wrong. They involve competing loyalties, fear of consequences, personal interests, and social expectations.
This is where the distinction between moral instruction and ethical education becomes important. Moral instruction may tell students what is right. Ethical education must help them understand why it is right, recognize competing considerations, and develop the courage to act accordingly.
Young people cannot develop sound judgment merely by memorizing moral lessons. They need opportunities to question, reflect, discuss difficult situations, and learn from the consequences of their decisions.
Ethical development begins at home, long before formal education starts. Parents and family members shape attitudes towards honesty, responsibility, empathy, and respect. Children observe how adults behave, resolve disagreements, and practise the principles they teach.
The wider social environment is equally influential. When honesty is rewarded, institutions operate fairly, and wrongdoing carries consequences, young citizens receive a powerful message about integrity. Conversely, when dishonesty appears to bring success without accountability, the credibility of ethical instruction is weakened.
Schools and universities cannot work in isolation. They must be part of a broader national effort involving families, communities, businesses, civil society, and public institutions.
Educational institutions nevertheless have a unique responsibility. They bring together students from diverse backgrounds and provide opportunities to develop cooperation, fairness, critical thinking, and respect for others.
Character formation is not an optional activity to be undertaken after the syllabus has been completed. It is an integral part of education itself.
One important step is to strengthen the place of ethics in the national curriculum, from primary school through higher education.
This need not require a separate subject at every level. Ethical reasoning can be incorporated into literature, history, science, business studies, social sciences, and technology.
Science lessons can explore the responsibilities associated with scientific discoveries. Business education can examine conflicts of interest, fair competition, and corruption. History can encourage reflection on injustice and the abuse of power. Technology education can address privacy, misinformation, cyberbullying, and artificial intelligence.
Students should regularly encounter realistic dilemmas that require them to weigh competing choices. Is it acceptable to share an unverified story because it supports a cause they believe in? Should a company compromise environmental protection to reduce costs? How should a manager respond when a senior colleague requests an improper favour?
Complex situations do not always have simple answers. What matters is that students learn to identify relevant facts, consider who may be affected, evaluate competing principles, anticipate consequences, and justify their decisions.
Such an approach develops independent judgment rather than unquestioning conformity. It also teaches students that respectful disagreement, supported by reason, is essential to ethical thinking.
No education reform can succeed without teachers. They are not merely transmitters of knowledge; they are role models whose conduct can leave a lasting impression.
A teacher who treats students fairly, acknowledges mistakes, rejects favouritism, and listens to differing opinions demonstrates integrity far more effectively than a lecture on moral values.
Teacher training should therefore equip educators to facilitate ethical discussions, manage disagreements constructively, and encourage independent thought. Teachers must be able to address difficult questions without imposing personal prejudices or discouraging legitimate criticism.
Schools must also practise what they teach. If students hear that fairness matters but observe arbitrary punishment, preferential treatment or humiliation, the lesson becomes contradictory.
If they are encouraged to speak honestly but punished for respectfully questioning an unfair decision, they may learn silence rather than integrity.
Ethical education is credible only when institutional behaviour reflects institutional values.
In Bangladesh, considerable importance is attached to examination results, grades, certificates, and admission to prestigious institutions. These priorities are understandable in a competitive society where educational qualifications influence employment and social mobility.
However, when academic success becomes the overriding objective, the means of achieving it may receive insufficient attention. Excessive pressure can encourage cheating, unhealthy competition, fear of failure, and the belief that results matter more than learning.
We must reconsider how we define educational achievement.
Academic standards should remain high, but they must be accompanied by a culture that values honesty, collaboration, curiosity, responsibility, and perseverance.
Assessment can place greater emphasis on research, group projects, presentations, practical problem-solving, and reflection, supported by robust safeguards against plagiarism and cheating.
Students should understand that failure, when approached honestly, can be a valuable learning experience. A student who admits a mistake and tries to correct it may demonstrate greater character than one who achieves a higher mark through dishonest means.
The objective is not to weaken competition, but to ensure that competition does not come at the expense of character.
Ethical judgment becomes meaningful when translated into action. Educational institutions should provide opportunities for students to practise responsibility beyond academic exercises.
Community service, environmental projects, voluntary work, peer mentoring, and initiatives supporting disadvantaged groups can cultivate empathy and civic responsibility. Such experiences help students understand the circumstances of people whose lives differ from their own.
Schools and universities could organize student-led projects addressing waste management, public health awareness, digital literacy, educational inequality, and social inclusion.
These activities must not become another exercise for collecting certificates. Their value lies in meaningful participation, reflection, and accountability. Students should consider what they have learned, whose lives they have affected, and what they could have done differently.
Service, when approached thoughtfully, develops both social awareness and moral maturity.
In my earlier writing on public-private partnership in education, I argued that the government and the private sector can complement each other in expanding educational opportunities and improving quality. This principle is equally relevant to ethical education.
Businesses have a direct interest in developing employees and leaders who understand integrity, accountability, fair competition, and responsible decision-making. Universities, employers, professional associations, and civil society organizations could collaborate on practical ethics programs, internships, mentoring, and case studies based on real professional challenges.
Business leaders could share experiences involving difficult decisions affecting customers, employees, suppliers, and society. Professional institutions could help integrate ethical standards into medicine, engineering, law, accounting, management, and information technology.
Such partnerships, however, must serve the public interest rather than commercial priorities alone. Ethical education should not become corporate public relations or a vehicle for promoting particular interests.
The government must establish appropriate standards, while educational institutions retain academic independence and ensure equal access to opportunities. The private sector can contribute resources and experience, but nurturing responsible citizens remains a collective responsibility.
Rapid technological development presents new challenges. Today's students must learn not only how to use technology, but also how to use it responsibly.
Artificial intelligence can support learning, research, and creativity, but it raises questions about plagiarism, intellectual honesty, privacy, misinformation, bias, and accountability.
Students must understand the difference between using a tool to enhance their thinking and using it to misrepresent someone else's work as their own.
Digital citizenship should therefore be an essential part of education. Young people must learn to verify information before sharing it, respect privacy, recognize harmful online behaviour, and understand that digital actions can have real-world consequences.
Technology can provide answers with extraordinary speed. It cannot, by itself, determine which answers are fair, humane, or socially responsible. That responsibility remains with human beings.
Assessing the effectiveness of ethical education presents a challenge. Character cannot be reliably measured through a single examination or reduced to a numerical score.
Nevertheless, institutions can examine whether their environments encourage fairness, respect, inclusion, and constructive dialogue. They can assess how complaints are handled, whether students feel safe reporting misconduct, how academic integrity is maintained, and whether opportunities are distributed fairly.
Reflective journals, discussions, project evaluations, and peer feedback can help students examine their own decisions. These approaches should support learning, not label individuals as morally superior or inferior.
Bangladesh could develop a practical national framework for ethical education, supported by teacher development, institutional guidance, and periodic evaluation. The emphasis should be on continuous improvement rather than imposing a rigid or politically-influenced definition of morality.
Ethical education must encourage independent thought while respecting cultural diversity, constitutional principles, human dignity, and the equal rights of all citizens.
Ultimately, an education system should be judged not only by the number of graduates it produces, but also by the kind of society those graduates help create.
Bangladesh needs entrepreneurs who pursue profit without exploiting people, public servants who treat public resources as a trust, professionals who uphold standards under pressure, and citizens who defend fairness even when doing so offers no immediate personal advantage.
We need young people who question authority without disrespect, express disagreement without hatred, compete without dishonesty, and pursue ambition without losing compassion.
This is not an argument for replacing scientific knowledge, technological competence, or economic ambition with moral instruction. It is an argument for bringing them together.
The most valuable education combines knowledge with wisdom, ambition with responsibility, and individual achievement with a commitment to the common good.
The journey must begin at home, continue in our schools and universities, and be reinforced by the conduct of our leaders and institutions. It requires sustained commitment, not merely a policy announcement.
Bangladesh has every reason to aspire to world-class education. But world-class education must mean more than internationally competitive degrees, advanced laboratories, and employable graduates. It must also mean developing people who can be trusted with knowledge, authority, wealth, and responsibility.
Our ultimate objective should be to nurture a generation that possesses not merely the intelligence to succeed, but the ethical compass to decide what success should mean.
A nation advances most sustainably when its people know not only how to get ahead, but also how to do so without compromising their integrity. That is the education Bangladesh must strive to provide for its next generation.
A Gafur is a Private Sector Professional and Writer, and Former Executive Director, The American Chamber of Commerce in Bangladesh (AmCham Bangladesh).

item.title: How exposed is Bangladesh to a prolonged Saudi crisis?. [ dawn ]
item.description:
Bangladesh is unlikely to see an immediate fall in remittances from Saudi Arabia even as Houthi attacks on the kingdom intensified from early October, but a slowdown in new migration could weigh on inflows in the years ahead.

Following the attacks, migration to Saudi Arabia, the largest destination for Bangladeshi workers, has already been disrupted. As of Sunday, 144 direct and transit flights had been affected by prolonged flight restrictions at Saudi airports, disrupting the travel plans of around 22,000 passengers.

But economists and manpower experts say remittance inflows are unlikely to be hit immediately because newly arrived migrant workers typically take about a year to start sending significant amounts of money home.

According to them, the longer-term impact will depend on the duration of the crisis, the performance of the Saudi economy and demand for labour, particularly in construction.

A prolonged crisis that damages the Saudi economy could slow job creation and reduce workers’ incomes. But the outcome is not necessarily negative for the kingdom’s economy.

If Houthi missile and drone attacks continue without damaging oilfields and refineries, higher global oil prices could boost Saudi revenues, potentially supporting investment and demand for foreign workers, according to Zahid Hussain, a former lead economist at the World Bank’s Dhaka office.

“But everything is uncertain so far,” he commented.

Remittances are a major source of foreign currency for Bangladesh, accounting for around 7.5 per cent of gross domestic product, according to World Bank data. Their importance has grown amid volatility in global energy markets following the US-Israel war on Iran, which has sent shockwaves through sectors ranging from agriculture to the garment industry.

In the July-September quarter of the current fiscal year, Saudi Arabia remained Bangladesh’s largest source of remittances. Inflows from the kingdom rose to $1.65 billion, up from $1.23bn in the same period of FY26, according to Bangladesh Bank data.

The kingdom accounted for 19.2pc of Bangladesh’s total remittance inflows in the first quarter of FY27, compared with 16.26pc a year earlier.

During the July-September quarter, overall remittances reached around $8.59bn, with Gulf Cooperation Council (GCC) countries continuing to account for the bulk of transfers.

Diversifying overseas jobs is becoming urgent

The latest disruption shows Bangladesh’s heavy reliance on a handful of overseas labour markets, leaving migrant workers and the economy exposed to regional crises.

Since FY2014-15, Saudi Arabia has employed around half of the 9.6 million Bangladeshis who went abroad for work. Workers in the kingdom have sent home an average of $5bn a year.

The pressure on migration is already evident. Overseas employment fell 36pc year-on-year to 134,000 in the July-August period this year, following a decline to around 969,000 workers in FY26, the lowest level in five years, according to Bureau of Manpower, Employment and Training data.

Tasneem Siddiqui, executive director of the Refugee and Migratory Movements Research Unit (RMMRU), a local think tank, said the crisis exposed the structural weaknesses of the country’s migration sector.

“Therefore, rather than relying on piecemeal decisions, we must completely overhaul and diversify the manpower market. Otherwise, one crisis after another will emerge, leaving us perpetually vulnerable,” said Tasneem, also a political science professor at Dhaka University.

She said the government needs a long-term strategy to develop skills suited to specific overseas markets and expand employment opportunities beyond traditional destinations.

“Long-term strategic planning is essential. Particularly, allocating a mere 0.08pc of the budget for a $35bn remittance sector is grossly insufficient to accomplish meaningful interventions,” she said.

Meanwhile, economist Zahid said Bangladesh should target countries facing ageing populations and labour shortages, including Japan and countries in eastern Europe, where demand for workers in nursing, caregiving and manufacturing could offer alternatives to Middle Eastern markets.

Sayema Haque Bidisha, an economics professor at Dhaka University, also called for greater diversification of migration destinations, stronger diplomatic engagement and better support for expatriates through overseas missions.

She said Bangladesh needs to improve its international image by demonstrating that its workers can fill skilled jobs, rather than being seen primarily as a source of manual labour.

Shariful Hasan, associate director of BRAC’s Migration Programme and Youth Platform, said earlier this month that many Bangladeshi workers in Saudi Arabia depend on daily or weekly employment and that security concerns have reduced work opportunities.

Pakistan faces greater exposure than India

Bangladesh is not the only country with a significant reliance on remittances from Saudi Arabia.

Its neighbours India and Pakistan also depend on money sent home by their citizens working in the kingdom, although the potential impact varies.

Saudi Arabia is Pakistan’s largest source of remittances, contributing $9.78 billion in the last fiscal year, according to State Bank of Pakistan data.

Meanwhile, around 7pc of India’s international remittance inflows originate from Saudi Arabia. The country receives about $8 billion annually from the kingdom, according to the Reserve Bank of India.

A prolonged crisis that affects employment and earnings in Saudi Arabia could therefore have a greater impact on Pakistan than on India, given Pakistan’s substantial reliance on the kingdom as a source of remittances.

Supporting migrant workers better. [ dhakatribune ]
item.description:
Despite the enormous contribution of migrant workers to our economy, it is a shame that Bangladesh still lacks an effective system for grading recruitment agencies, leaving prospective migrants with little reliable information about whom they can trust.
This failure, recently acknowledged by State Minister for Expatriates’ Welfare and Overseas Employment Md Nurul Haque Nur yesterday, demands our urgent attention.
Thousands of workers invest their savings, sell land, or borrow heavily to secure overseas employment. Many are subsequently confronted with excessive recruitment fees, misleading job offers, and working conditions that differ sharply from what they were promised.
It should be understood that a licence alone cannot be treated as proof that an agency is competent, ethical, or deserving of public trust.
Agencies must be rigorously evaluated across key metrics: Recruitment practices, fee transparency, complaint histories, regulatory compliance, as well as post-placement worker protection.
These assessments should also be publicly accessible, allowing prospective migrants to make informed decisions.
However, grading alone will not solve the problem. The government must strengthen monitoring, investigate complaints promptly, and impose meaningful penalties on agencies that exploit workers.
Those repeatedly found guilty of misconduct should face licence suspension or cancellation, while victims must have access to compensation and legal assistance.
Bangladesh also needs to move away from a system that prioritizes the expansion of recruitment businesses over the quality of their services.
More agencies do not necessarily mean more opportunities, particularly when weak oversight allows unscrupulous operators to thrive. What matters is having reliable agencies that connect workers with legitimate employers at reasonable costs.
Our responsibility must also extend beyond the airport. Bangladesh's diplomatic missions should provide effective support to expatriates facing wage theft, contract violations, and workplace abuse.
Migrant workers are not merely sources of remittance income; they are citizens whose labour and sacrifices deserve protection. Building a trustworthy recruitment system is therefore a fundamental obligation to the people who help sustain our economy.

item.title: Caring for the carers. [ dhakatribune ]
item.description:
In Bangladesh, where women shoulder most household responsibilities, the International Day of Care and Support observed today should remind us that caring for others is a shared social responsibility, not an obligation that falls disproportionately on women.
Care work is among the most essential contributions to society, yet it remains among the least recognized.
Bangladesh’s first Time-Use Survey, conducted in 2021 by the Bangladesh Bureau of Statistics (BBS), revealed that women spend roughly seven times as much time on unpaid domestic and care work as men.
Cooking, cleaning, raising children, and caring for sick or elderly family members sustain households and enable others to pursue education and employment.
Yet this labour unfortunately remains largely invisible in economic calculations, and is often dismissed as an ordinary part of being a woman.
The consequences are significant: Women who devote hours to unpaid work have less time to pursue paid employment, develop professional skills, or participate in public life. Those who work outside the home often face a second shift of domestic responsibilities, with little support or recognition.
Meanwhile, domestic workers and other care professionals frequently face low wages, insecure employment, and inadequate protection.
Encouragingly, Bangladesh has taken an important step towards recognizing this contribution through a commitment in the FY2025-26 national budget to include the economic value of women's unpaid labour in GDP calculations.
However, this recognition must lead to meaningful change. Affordable childcare, accessible support for elderly and disabled people, stronger protections for domestic workers, and policies encouraging men to share household responsibilities are essential.
The government, employers, and communities must work together to build a care system that supports both caregivers and those who need care. Families, too, must challenge the assumption that care is naturally women's work.
Care is indispensable to our economy and society, and we would do well to understand that properly valuing it -- as well as the people providing it -- is a matter of fairness, dignity, and sustainable development.

item.title: The 18 months that changed Bangladesh. [ dhakatribune ]
item.description:
In August 2024, the streets of Dhaka smelled of smoke and uncertainty. Autorickshaws fell silent. Shopkeepers pulled down shutters early. The old order had collapsed, and in its place stepped an 84-year-old Nobel laureate who promised to shepherd Bangladesh toward democracy.
Eighteen months later, in February 2026, those same streets erupted in celebration. The BNP won a sweeping victory, and Tarique Rahman was sworn in as prime minister. The transition felt complete, a return to the democratic fold after an unelected interregnum.
But as we mark eight months of the new government, a question lingers: What exactly happened during those 18 months?
The Yunus-led interim government departed, handing over power with farewell speeches about sovereignty and dignity. Yet they left behind a trail of shadowy decisions and unanswered questions.
They governed without an electoral mandate but with immense moral authority, born of a mass uprising. That authority came with an obligation: To be more transparent than any elected government, not less.
We have crossed the bridge back to democracy. But the bridge itself was built with materials that now demand inspection. It is time to light a torch and walk back into that tunnel.
The ledger of lost lives
The most damning indictment of the interim government’s priorities is written in the bodies of dead children.
Bangladesh is now in the grip of the world’s worst measles outbreak. Starting mid-March, over 200,000 have been hospitalized across the country, with the overall death toll from the ongoing outbreak being 1,242 as of today. 94% of them were children under five.
In Sylhet, Amin Mia sold the family’s autorickshaw to pay for hospital treatment for his two-year-old son, Arman. The boy died unvaccinated in July. “They came only after I buried my son,” Mia said.
In Chhatak, Humayun Rashid’s nine-month-old daughter Labiba died in June. She was eligible for vaccination in April, when the emergency program lowered the age threshold to six months. “No health worker came to tell us,” her father said.
The outbreak was preventable. In September 2025, the interim government stopped purchasing vaccines through UNICEF -- a reliable system that had worked for years -- and switched to an open tender system, a move widely suspected to be a precursor to privatizing vaccine procurement.
The tender stalled. Vaccine stock depleted. A planned nationwide campaign was cancelled. By 2025, first-dose coverage had fallen to 90% and second-dose to 86%, both below the 95% threshold needed for herd immunity.
The current government reinstated Unicef procurement and launched an emergency campaign in April. But the response has been incomplete.
A Reuters investigation found that the campaign’s target list excluded four million children in the eligible age group. By August, the proportion of confirmed cases who were unvaccinated had actually risen, from 82% to 85%.
The children who died were failed twice: First by the procurement decision, then by the response to its consequences.
The architecture of opacity
When Yunus addressed the nation in those first days, he spoke of transparency. He promised that all advisers would disclose their assets. That promise gathered dust like an abandoned building.
Instead, what emerged was a pattern of decisions that benefited entities intimately connected to the chief adviser himself.
Within two months of Yunus taking office, the National Board of Revenue granted Grameen Bank a five-year income tax exemption until 2029, reversing a 2020 decision. Based on previous records, the bank used to pay around Tk 200 crore annually in taxes, meaning the total revenue loss to the government over five years is estimated to exceed Tk 1,000 crore.
Grameen University, established by Yunus, received approval within three months of applying, while applications from at least 22 other private universities remained pending for years.
Then came the legal reckoning. In September 2026, the High Court ordered Grameen Kalyan, founded by Yunus, to pay Tk 666 crore in outstanding taxes for 2012 through 2017.
The court rejected the organization’s writ petitions, paving the way for the NBR to collect. Jurist Shahdeen Malik said there would be “a certain perception” about the facilities received and that “conflict of interest is another dimension which should have been considered more seriously.”
Transparency International Bangladesh warned that reforms initiated by the interim government had “largely failed” to ensure institutional independence and accountability. TIB concluded that resistance from entrenched interests had derailed much of the interim government’s reform agenda.
The politics of rewriting the past
Perhaps nothing reveals the interim government’s political project more clearly than its enabling of historical erasure.
On February 5, 2025, crowds responding to social media calls for a “bulldozer procession” systematically dismantled the Bangabandhu Memorial Museum at Dhanmondi 32, the historic residence of Sheikh Mujibur Rahman.
The crowd first vandalized and set fire to the museum around 8:30 pm, and by 11:10 pm, an excavator had been brought to the site. Police had deployed additional forces but “did not create any major obstacles to those moving to the museum in processions.”
The interim government issued a statement calling the events “unexpected and unintended.” Transparency International Bangladesh criticized the government’s “alarming nonchalance.”
A case petition was filed against 27 individuals including Yunus and former law adviser Asif Nazrul. The court dismissed it for “lack of grounds.” No arrests have been made. The accused remain free.
The first demolition occurred under the interim government. The precedent was set in February 2025, when an unelected government with a moral mandate to uphold justice stood by while a national museum was demolished by mobs.
The geopolitical gamble
In his farewell address, Yunus declared that Bangladesh had restored its “sovereignty, national interest, and dignity” in foreign policy. But what did this rhetorical sovereignty actually mean in practice?
On February 9, 2026, just three days before the general election, the interim government signed the US-Bangladesh Agreement on Reciprocal Trade. An analysis of the 32-page agreement found a sharp imbalance in its language: “Bangladesh shall” appears 131 times, while “US shall” appears just six times.
The agreement requires Bangladesh to align with US sanctions regimes, accept US regulatory standards for agricultural products, relax foreign ownership limits in key sectors, and accede to a long list of international intellectual property treaties within specified timelines.
It also embeds binding procurement commitments: 14 Boeing aircraft, approximately $15 billion in American LNG offtake, and 700,000 metric tons of US wheat annually.
The agreement was signed by a government with no electoral mandate, three days before the people it governed were given the chance to choose their own representatives. By what authority did an unelected administration bind the nation to these terms?
The republic’s right to know
An unelected government has no built-in accountability mechanisms. No parliament to answer to. No opposition to monitor its actions. That is precisely why the Yunus government bore a special obligation, a moral obligation, to be more transparent than any elected government could be expected to be.
Yet over 18 months, serious allegations of corruption and abuse of power were raised against several advisers. And they were met with little visible response.
TIB’s Corruption Perceptions Index for 2025 showed Bangladesh’s score rising by only one point to 24, the second-lowest in 14 years. TIB stated that the interim government “failed to take effective and exemplary measures against corruption” and that money laundering had not stopped.
This is not a call for prosecution. It is a call for disclosure. Publish the full text and annexes of the trade agreement. Publish the vaccine procurement timeline. Publish the tax exemption list. Publish the chain of command on Dhanmondi 32.
If the documents show nothing, the interim government is vindicated. If they show something, the public learns what was done in its name. Disclosure does not require a tribunal. It requires a government willing to release paper.
The interim government is gone. But its decisions are not. The trade agreement runs for years. The tax exemptions run to 2029. The measles outbreak is ongoing. The demolition is permanent.
The silence of the current government on these matters is itself part of the story. Why has the new government not repealed the trade agreement, investigated the procurement, or pursued the Dhanmondi 32 case?
The audit demand is not directed only at Yunus. It is directed at whoever currently holds the power to disclose and chooses not to.
We call for a parliamentary commission to review every foreign agreement signed during this period. We call for the full list of tax exemptions received by Yunus and connected institutions to be made public. We call for a full accounting of the vaccine procurement decisions that led to the measles outbreak. The children who died deserve nothing less. And we call for an investigation into the demolition of Dhanmondi 32: Who gave the order, and why no one was held accountable.
These investigations are not intended to defame Yunus or his advisers. They are required in the interest of the nation itself. Examining this interim administration’s powers, responsibilities, and shortcomings can help establish a framework for future caretaker governments. We must assess where mistakes were made or limits exceeded so that similar problems can be avoided in the future.
The citizens of Bangladesh, who braved bullets in July 2024, who demanded democracy, who sacrificed for a better future, deserve nothing less.
They own this republic. They have a right to know what was done in their name during those 18 months when decisions were made in the dark.
The sun has risen on a new government. But shadows remain. Let us chase them out, together.
Zakir Kibria is a Bangladeshi writer, policy analyst and entrepreneur based in Kathmandu, Nepal. His email address is zakir.kibria@gmail.com . Views expressed are the writer’s own.

item.title: Who cares for the carers?. [ dhakatribune ]
item.description:
Most of us have looked after someone who is ill. Even a short illness brings constant questions: Have they had something to drink? Can they wash themselves? Have they slept?
Now imagine asking those questions every day, for years, while caring for a daughter with a disability, a parent with dementia, or a relative with a serious mental health condition.
For unpaid family carers, this is their reality.
They care with love and commitment at enormous personal cost. Their health, livelihoods, education, and social lives can be pushed aside. They hold communities together and sustain health and care systems without pay, recognition, or even a break.
Bangladesh has valued unpaid household and care work at Tk6.7 trillion in 2021, approximately 18.9% of GDP. The calculation includes unpaid domestic work as well as care, but it reveals the scale of a contribution that is too often overlooked.
Bangladesh’s National Healthy Ageing Strategy and Action Plan 2024-2030 acknowledges that family carers can delay or prevent the need for residential care for older people.
Yet recognition in principle is not the same as support in practice. Assistance may go to a person with a disability through the disability allowance or to a household through the Family Card. Too often, nobody looks beneath the surface. Carers are frequently the very people navigating applications and managing payments intended to support someone else.
The evidence from our work in Bangladesh is striking. Through our partnership with the Centre for Disability in Development (CDD), research in a project area in Savar found that 67% of households with a carer and a person with a disability were living in extreme poverty, on less than $1 a day.
Separate research highlighted that 95% of family carers in Savar had a health issue or disability of their own. These findings are local, not national estimates, but they expose the pressures hidden behind the word “care.”
Caring has a profoundly disproportionate impact on women. In our three-year program with CDD in Savar, 93% of the 1,008 unpaid family carers supported were women and girls.
For many, caring means giving up paid work, perpetuating financial dependence, and having little time to look after themselves. When we fail to support carers, we deepen inequality for women and girls too.
Consider Kohinoor, a mother in Dhaka caring for her daughter Farea, who has autism. She once struggled alone. Joining a local carers group connected her with people who understood, and she eventually became its president.
With livelihood training, she started poultry rearing. Within two months, her flock had grown from five birds to 12, and she was earning money by selling eggs.
Kohinoor is not an isolated success. Working with CDD, Carers Worldwide has supported 1,008 carers in Savar, established 50 carers groups and trained 425 carers in income-generating activities. Six community caring centres offered children with disabilities care and learning opportunities while giving their carers precious time for work, rest, and social connection.
An independent evaluation found that 98% of participating carers reported improvements in their physical and/or mental health. These numbers represent people moving from isolation towards friendship, from financial insecurity towards opportunity, and from being overlooked towards being heard.
There are encouraging signs of wider change. Carers ID cards introduced in Dhaka last year acknowledge the contribution carers make and help them access priority services.
Salma, a recipient, said: “Within my family and society, I was without recognition. Now, my value and recognition within my family have increased.” The initiative aims to reach more than a thousand carers.
Bangladesh has a chance to lead. New social protection systems must identify unpaid family carers, not only the people receiving care, and recognize the financial costs they bear.
Health services should offer carers medical care, mental health support, and respite. Flexible livelihoods and carers’ groups should be part of community development, and carers themselves must have a voice in shaping policy.
The community volunteer network proposed in the National Healthy Ageing Strategy offers a promising starting point. It could finally provide an answer to parents who ask: “Who will care for my loved one when I am no longer here?”
This approach deserves a place in the broader National Health Policy, so that support extends beyond older people to families caring for people with disabilities and long-term conditions.
On the International Day of Care and Support, October 29, we should celebrate carers’ extraordinary contribution. But gratitude is not enough.
The real measure of progress is whether someone like Kohinoor can care for her daughter without sacrificing her own health and future. We must make that support a right, not a matter of chance.
Those who care for others deserve care too. It is time for Bangladesh to care for the carers.
Anil Patil is the Founder and Executive Director of Carers Worldwide. Anil has 25 years’ experience in the international development sector as a veterinarian, development worker, grant maker, and trustee.

item.title: A prisoner list is not protection. [ dhakatribune ]
item.description:
The execution of two Bangladeshi citizens in Saudi Arabia's Makkah province on October 14, 2026, raises a challenging question: What is the purpose of consular protection if the government is unable to determine which of its nationals are at risk of execution until it is too late?
According to Saudi officials, two people, Nazerul Islam Abdul Basir and Siti Akhter, have been sentenced to death after a court found them guilty of alleged immoral behavior in a mosque.
The Bangladesh consulate in Jeddah stated that it had not received advance notice of the executions. Further study found a disturbing feature. Saudi officials furnished them with a roster of nearly 2,500 offenders, including their names, but not details of their capital sentences.
Under Article 36 of the 1963 Vienna Convention on Consular Relations, foreign nationals in detention have the right to communicate with and have access to consular officials.
If a detained citizen requests consular aid, the consular post shall be notified without delay, and the detainee shall be informed of this right.
Article 37(a) concerns the notification of the death of a foreign national, if the receiving authorities have the essential information. The Convention does not oblige a state to give prior notification of every execution to be carried out. Whether it violated them depends on confidential variables such as the conditions of imprisonment and whether consular notice was requested.
Bangladesh should obtain the required information rather than bring a bogus legal accusation. A bilateral system needs to be created for prompt notification of capital charges, death sentences, appeals, and scheduled executions.
The amount of Bangladesh's reliance on Saudi Arabia makes this a serious matter. In 2025, the Bureau of Manpower, Employment, and Training stated that 752,715 Bangladeshis sought employment in Saudi Arabia. Saudi Arabia remained the greatest provider of remittances to Bangladesh in fiscal year 2025-26, totalling more than $5.85 billion.
The enumeration named the two executed individuals but made no mention of the imposition of death sentences. The reported offenses prevented consular officials from reliably associating the entries with the executions.
It cannot guide a task that requires immediate engagement unless it specifies the allegation, the phase of processes, the verdict, the status of appeals, and the next important date.
Other nations demonstrate the operation of various components inside such a system. The Migrant Workers and Overseas Filipinos Act of the Philippines creates a Legal Assistant for Migrant Workers' Affairs and a Legal Assistance Fund to reimburse qualified expenses such as foreign attorney fees and litigation costs.
Its relevance stems from the distribution of accountability and funding for legal action, rather than relying on improvised remedies. India's MADAD consular grievance portal offers a unique feature: Citizens can lodge grievances and track their progress within the government's consular framework.
Although grievance monitoring alone cannot prevent an execution, a similar platform could enable Bangladesh to record detention conditions, assign tasks, verify timetables, and escalate lingering issues.
Indonesia provides a warning example. Siti Zainab, an Indonesian domestic servant, was executed in Saudi Arabia in 2015, despite efforts by Indonesian MPs to secure a pardon and Jakarta's concerns about the lack of prior information to her family and diplomatic authorities.
The example demonstrates that diplomatic entreaties alone cannot ensure security. Robust precautions must be taken before a problem reaches a critical stage.
For someone accused of a capital crime, time is more than just a bureaucratic issue. Timely consular intervention can help educate families, find a suitable local attorney, provide translation assistance, obtain judicial rulings, and track appeal deadlines.
It may also provide authorities with an opportunity to consider clemency or alternative sentencing, depending on the area's legislation. These opportunities are lost as the execution begins.
Bangladesh cannot assume that every conviction is invalid and cannot ask Saudi courts to abandon jurisdiction. However, it may be argued that consular protection is important and that families are not left to seek necessary answers following an irreversible ruling. Advising migrants to follow the laws of their host country is risky because it does not provide them with legal protection if arrested.
Bangladesh should demand the full judicial records of both events and provide families with verifiable information. There needs to be a proper internal evaluation of the measures to receive, evaluate, and implement the list of inmates.
Dhaka and Riyadh should set up a formal bilateral consular mechanism, whereby they would be required to inform on important criminal allegations, death sentences, appellate rulings, and scheduled executions in a timely manner.
In high-risk scenarios, Bangladesh should have an accurate, up-to-date list of the incarcerated citizens and identified authorities. Each record shall contain the name of the inmate, the charge, the judicial status, the sentence, the legal counsel, and the pertinent dates.
Create a dedicated fund for legal aid to support local lawyers, provide translation services, and hasten legal reviews. The number of detainees supported, the number of cases raised, and the outcomes should be regularly reported to the public, while respecting the confidentiality of personal information.
Bangladesh can learn from the Philippines’ financial framework and India’s case-monitoring system, but neither can be rolled out immediately. The Indonesian situation indicates that diplomatic protests after an execution don’t work. A strong system requires verifiable data from host countries, appropriate staffing and finance at foreign missions, and clear accountability in Dhaka.
In my 2020 Op-Ed for the Dhaka Tribune, "Is anyone listening?" I highlighted my concern for the safety of Bangladeshi citizens whose livelihoods rely on migration. That is the inquiry.
A prisoner roster is useless unless it motivates people to act. Bangladesh must ensure that when an individual receives a death sentence abroad, the diplomatic mission is promptly alerted so that it can investigate, acquire legal aid, and pursue all available options.
Md Fahmedul Islam Dewan is a Lecturer, Department of Law, World University of Bangladesh.

Education must remain inclusive. [ dhakatribune ]
item.description:
We agree with Education and Primary and Mass Education Minister Dr ANM Ehsanul Hoque Milon that religious education can play a significant role in shaping more responsible citizens.
Integrating moral values, integrity, and spiritual literacy into national curricula can certainly help stem social degradation and foster conscientious youth. Merely striving for efficiency and growth are meaningless if fellow citizens lack empathy and care.
With that said, in a nation built upon pluralism and constitutional guarantees of equal rights, regardless of one’s religion or faith, state policy regarding moral and religious education must strictly reflect our diverse national fabric.
If we are to educate our children about religion and faith, and expect them to be able to take the lessons they provide, then we must simultaneously ensure that no single faith receives majoritarian preference while neglecting the rest.
Bangladesh is home to millions of Hindu, Buddhist, Christian, and ethnic minority citizens, among other faiths, whose traditions and values are integral to our national identity.
As such, when state officials frame moral development through the prism of a single religion, they risk alienating minority students and eroding the inclusive foundation of public education.
Every child attending a state school or general institution deserves access to moral instruction that honours, reflects, and respects their own heritage and faith, rather than being subjected to a standardized framework that treats non-majority traditions as an afterthought.
Modernizing our national education system therefore requires a delicate balance between core ethical values and secular inclusivity.
While streamlining madrasa education with mainstream science, arts, and technology is a welcome effort to bridge structural disparities that have existed for too long, national policy must also ensure that general public schools remain welcoming spaces for students of all backgrounds.
A truly progressive curriculum must emphasize universal values -- integrity, tolerance, civic responsibility, and mutual respect -- alongside comprehensive, high-quality instruction regarding students’ respective faiths. That should be the goal.

item.title: Parties must prioritize national stability. [ dhakatribune ]
item.description:
The attack on the central office of the Communist Party of Bangladesh (CPB) in Dhaka’s Paltan area is a deeply disturbing reminder of the partisan hostility still poisoning our political landscape.
When political offices are stormed, vandalized, or targeted by mobs over alleged slogans or ideological grievances, democratic norms are fundamentally violated.
Reverting to street-level violence, intimidation, and reflexive mudslinging exposes a reckless disregard for civil order at a time when the nation can least afford political instability.
Instead of taking immediate responsibility or condemning mob behaviour, the immediate aftermath of the incident reduced to predictable finger-pointing, partisan denial, and blame-shifting.
This toxic reflex must end if we are to make any progress as a nation.
Political parties across the spectrum - whether in government or opposition - must recognize that their primary duty is to the citizens of Bangladesh, not to settle petty political scores or establish dominance through intimidation.
At a moment when the country is confronting severe economic pressures, turning political rivalries into physical clashes is an unpardonable distraction from the urgent work of national governance.
Allowing partisan mobs to operate with impunity under the guise of political grievance invites lawlessness and further fractures. Violence cannot be normalized as a tool for political expression.
Law enforcement agencies must investigate the Paltan attack with absolute impartiality, identifying and prosecuting the perpetrators regardless of their political affiliations.
The leadership of all political parties must also issue an unequivocal, zero-tolerance directive to their cadres against mob violence and political thuggery.
Bangladesh's democratic space has all but eroded, and we cannot think of reviving it if political dissent is met with bricks and iron rods. It is time for our political parties to focus their energies on what matters -- constructive policy, economic stabilization, and public service.

item.title: When the state turns humiliation into public spectacle. [ dhakatribune ]
item.description:
A person can be presumed innocent in a courtroom and condemned by thousands on a smartphone screen before the first hearing begins.
In Bangladesh, videos of police raids increasingly expose detained women, men, and even children to public scrutiny, often revealing their faces and personal circumstances before the allegations against them have been established.
What makes this practice particularly troubling is not merely the invasion of privacy, but the transformation of state authority into a source of public humiliation.
When law enforcement agencies facilitate such exposure and media outlets reproduce it without sufficient scrutiny, the distinction between investigating a crime and staging a spectacle begins to disappear.
The recent incident in Purbachal, where 85 people were detained during a raid and reportedly pressured to uncover their faces before cameras, illustrates the problem.
Similar footage from establishments in Gulshan and Uttara has circulated online, inviting audiences to speculate about the identities, occupations, and private lives of those detained.
Yet the central question is not whether the public should know about suspected wrongdoing. It is whether exposing the faces and personal circumstances of people who have not been convicted contributes anything meaningful to public understanding of the alleged offense.
This question matters because public humiliation is not an incidental consequence of these videos. It has become part of their appeal.
A raid offers the drama of sudden discovery, a group of detainees supplies the visual material, and a camera turns the encounter into content.
The audience is invited to feel that it has witnessed wrongdoing being punished, even when no court has determined that an offense occurred.
In this arrangement, suspicion becomes a form of guilt, exposure becomes a substitute for accountability, and humiliation acquires the appearance of justice.
The underlying danger is that punishment begins to precede the judicial process. A criminal investigation is supposed to establish facts, test evidence, and identify responsibility through lawful procedures. Publicly displaying detainees, by contrast, can impose a social penalty before those procedures have run their course.
A person may eventually be released, acquitted, or found to have had no involvement in the alleged offense, but the digital record remains. Images can be copied, reposted, downloaded, and detached from their original context. A subsequent correction rarely travels as far as the original accusation.
For women, the consequences can be particularly severe. Exposure may invite moral judgment, harassment, and reputational damage that extend to their families and professional lives.
In a society where women's conduct is frequently subjected to disproportionate scrutiny, the publication of footage from a police raid can function as an instrument of social punishment, regardless of the legal merits of the case.
Their identities become the story, while the evidence, the circumstances of the raid, and the conduct of the authorities receive comparatively less attention.
The result is a disturbing inversion of accountability: The people whose alleged conduct requires investigation become publicly identifiable, while the decisions of those exercising state power may remain largely unexamined.
Men are not immune to this practice. Videos of searches, phone inspections, and interrogations can expose private communications, personal associations, and intimate details to strangers.
Children face an even more alarming risk. The circulation of a schoolgirl's video following allegations about her private life demonstrates how quickly a moment of vulnerability can become a permanent public record.
Bangladesh's Children Act restricts the publication of information that may identify a child in circumstances covered by its provisions. Yet the existence of a legal prohibition does not automatically protect children when digital audiences reward exposure and those responsible for sharing the footage fail to consider its consequences.
The Constitution of Bangladesh provides important protections relevant to this debate. Article 31 concerns protection of the law and treatment in accordance with law, while Article 35 includes safeguards against compelled self-incrimination and torture or cruel, inhuman or degrading punishment.
The Universal Declaration of Human Rights also recognizes the presumption of innocence and protection against arbitrary interference with privacy, family, home, and reputation.
These principles are not suspended because someone has been detained or because a video attracts considerable attention. Nor does the public's curiosity automatically establish a public interest in revealing a person's identity.
The distinction between public interest and public curiosity deserves particular emphasis. Reporting that authorities have conducted a raid, detained individuals, or uncovered evidence of suspected wrongdoing may serve a legitimate public purpose.
Yet, identifying the people involved, broadcasting their faces, or displaying their distress requires a separate justification. Their identities may be relevant in some cases, particularly when authorities are seeking public assistance or when identification is necessary to understand a matter of genuine public importance.
But such exceptions should not become routine practice. The question should always be whether disclosure is necessary, proportionate, and supported by a clear public interest, rather than whether it is likely to generate attention.
This is where the conduct of media organizations becomes inseparable from the problem. Journalism cannot surrender its editorial judgment merely because footage comes from an official source.
Police briefings, photographs, and videos are not neutral windows into reality; they reflect decisions about what to record, what to disclose, and how an operation should be presented.
When journalists publish such material without asking why detainees are being exposed, whether the footage is necessary, or whether its circulation could cause disproportionate harm, they risk becoming distributors of an official narrative rather than independent observers of state power.
The economic and technological incentives of digital journalism make this failure easier to understand, though not to excuse.
Faces, confrontation, and apparent scandal attract clicks and shares. A video that invites moral condemnation may travel faster than a carefully reported account of investigative procedure or legal safeguards.
As mobile journalism and live broadcasting expand, the cost of recording and distributing an encounter has fallen dramatically.
Editorial restraint, however, has not necessarily advanced at the same pace. The result is an environment in which the capacity to expose people has grown faster than the willingness to consider whether they should be exposed.
There is also a serious institutional question for law enforcement. If journalists are informed about raids in advance, accompany officers, and receive footage from official sources, clear rules are needed to establish the limits of access and disclosure.
Recording material for evidentiary purposes is not equivalent to distributing it for publicity. A video may have legitimate investigative value while being entirely unsuitable for public release.
The authority to investigate suspected crime should not be treated as an unrestricted licence to display the people under investigation. If allegations of threats to expose detainees are substantiated, they demand especially serious scrutiny because the prospect of public disgrace could become a means of coercion or extortion.
Bangladesh's courts have previously raised concerns about presenting arrested persons and suspects before the media, including judicial interventions in 2012 and 2015 and observations concerning media briefings during ongoing investigations in 2019.
The persistence of similar practices suggests that judicial concern alone cannot establish an effective culture of restraint.
Clear operational rules, enforceable accountability, and consistent editorial standards are needed to translate legal principles into everyday practice.
Any policy should distinguish legitimate public disclosure from unnecessary identification, protect children and vulnerable people, and establish consequences for unauthorized or coercive dissemination of footage.
Ultimately, the issue is larger than the privacy of individual detainees. It concerns the kind of relationship citizens are permitted to have with the institutions that exercise power over them.
When an arrest becomes an opportunity for public shaming, the state communicates that dignity is conditional and that suspicion can strip a person of ordinary protections.
When media organizations amplify that message, they help normalize a culture in which exposure is mistaken for evidence and humiliation for justice.
HM Nazmul Alam is an academic, journalist, and political analyst based in Dhaka, Bangladesh. Currently he teaches at IUBAT.

item.title: Can Bangladesh’s cyber police outrun its institutions?. [ dhakatribune ]
item.description:
A police officer watching a crowded street sees only what is in front of them. A cyber police officer can potentially see patterns across thousands of phones, accounts, images, and videos.
Bangladesh is now developing the capacity to do much more of that.
On October 1, the country launched its new Cyber Police Unit with an approved structure of 4,592 posts. The unit is tasked with investigating cyber and financial crimes, analyzing digital evidence, monitoring social media and the dark web, and using AI-assisted video analytics and facial identification. Cyber desks are planned for police stations, alongside a 24/7 cyber support centre.
The case for expanding cyber policing is straightforward. Criminal activity increasingly leaves a digital trail, and police need the expertise and technology to follow it.
But a more capable cyber police force also raises a less comfortable question: Can the institutions governing these new powers develop as quickly as the powers themselves?
Digital policing is not merely about catching criminals more efficiently. It also concerns who can access information, how it is interpreted, and what happens when the state gets it wrong.
Bangladesh is not starting from scratch. The Criminal Investigation Department (CID) has operated its Cyber Police Centre since 2017 to deal with cybercrime and related digital investigations.
Since 2020, the Bangladesh Police’s Police Cyber Support for Women (PCSW) has provided legal and technological assistance to women facing cybercrime, including counselling and referrals to police stations, specialised units and victim-support centres. Broader reporting channels include police stations and the national emergency service, 999.
The challenge is not just creating more places for victims to report. It is making these channels work together.
A woman reporting image-based abuse, for example, should not have to know whether her case belongs with a local police station, a new cyber desk, the Cyber Police Centre, PCSW, or another specialized unit.
Her case should reach the right expertise without requiring her to navigate the bureaucracy herself.
That becomes more important as the new unit expands. The 4,592 figure represents approved posts, not a fully staffed force. Existing police personnel will initially fill positions before additional recruitment. The cyber desks and 24/7 support centre will also have to move from organisational plans to functioning services.
But the harder questions begin once the police have the data.
Who can access sensitive digital evidence? How long should it be retained? When can it be shared with another agency? How should investigators document the use of AI-assisted systems? And what happens when an automated identification or analysis is wrong?
A mistaken police conclusion about a digital identity, image, or online interaction can affect an investigation, a person’s reputation, or their freedom. As analytical tools become more powerful, scrutiny of their conclusions becomes more important.
Bangladesh’s Personal Data Protection Act 2026 establishes a broader framework for protecting personal data while allowing processing without consent where necessary for the prevention, detection, inquiry, investigation or prosecution of offences.
That is important for law enforcement. But a general data-protection framework cannot by itself determine how every police database, forensic system or AI-assisted tool should be operated.
Accountability matters especially because Bangladesh’s recent police oversight framework remains unsettled.
The 2025 Police Commission Ordinance included a mechanism for citizen complaints, but that framework is no longer in effect.
This creates a sequencing problem. It is relatively easy to acquire technology and create new police posts. It is harder to build durable institutions capable of scrutinizing how that technology is used.
Once databases, analytical systems, and specialized investigative practices become embedded, changing the rules around them becomes more difficult.
Bangladesh should build safeguards alongside capability. The new Cyber Police Unit should connect with existing victim-support and referral services rather than set up another isolated reporting channel.
Police should have clear operational rules governing access to, retention, and sharing of digital evidence, as well as procedures for documenting and challenging consequential errors in automated analysis. Citizens also need credible avenues to question misuse of digital investigative powers.
The future of cyber policing will not be determined only by what police can see. It will be determined by what they are allowed to do with what they see, and whether citizens have meaningful ways to challenge them when they get it wrong.
Ashfaq Ferdous is an academic at Southeast University, Bangladesh, and a former Assistant Superintendent of Police with Bangladesh Police.

item.title: Starc takes six as Australia fight back in South Africa decider. [ dawn ]
item.description:
Mitchell Starc said a “reset at lunch” led to an Australian fightback after South Africa made a flying start on the first day of the third Test at Newlands on Tuesday.

Starc finished with six for 72 as South Africa were bowled out for 329 shortly before the close in a match which will decide a series between the two leading Test nations.

It was a performance which looked unlikely as South Africa raced to 140 without loss at lunch after being sent in.

Starc was one of the bowlers punished, with the tall left-arm pacer conceding 39 runs in seven overs, including four successive boundaries by Marques Ackerman, who went on to score a rapid 95.

“We probably expected more out of the wicket,” said Starc. “It was quite slow, with tennis ball bounce. They came at us hard.

“We didn’t have our best stuff in the first two hours but the last two sessions were right up there. It’s what we expect from this group. We had a reset at lunch and just tried to change the momentum in the field.”

Ackerman, playing in his second Test, took the fight to the Australian bowlers with some dazzling strokes.

The slightly-built left-hander was on 82 not out at lunch, scored off just 75 balls.

He attacked veteran off-spinner Nathan Lyon, dancing down the pitch and hitting him over the stand at midwicket for six. But he tried one shot too many after lunch and was stranded when Lyon pushed the ball wider, giving Alex Carey an easy stumping.

Ackerman, 30, said South Africa would probably have been happy if they had been offered a total of 329 before play.

But he admitted: “We probably left a few runs out there.”

Ackerman, who won a place in the side through strong domestic performances and some big scores for South Africa A, including 256 against Bangladesh A in August, is not normally an opening batsman but said he was not troubled by the adjustment.

“I have quite often had to face a new ball in my career and playing against our own fast bowlers in the nets has been good preparation,” he said.

item.description:
Defending champions Pakistan on Tuesday announced a 15-member squad for the U-19 Asia Cup, which will be held in Oman from Nov 5 to 14.

Farhan Yousuf will lead the side, which is scheduled to depart for Oman from Karachi on Oct 29, the Pakistan Cricket Board (PCB) said in a statement.

Pakistan have been placed in Group ‘A’ alongside India, Nepal and hosts the United Arab Emirates (UAE) in the eight-team tournament.

The squad includes wicket-keeper-batters Abdul Qadir and Hamza Zahoor, and batters Usman Khan, Hayam Khan, Jahangir Bilal and Huzaifa Ahsan. All-rounders Ahmed Hussain and Hasnain Abbas Dar have also been included.

The pace attack comprises Abdul Subhan, Mohammad Seyam, Ali Raza and Rizwanullah, while Mohammad Huzaifa and Niqab Shafiq are the two frontline spin options.

Of the 15 players selected for the continental event, only Ali Raza and Huzaifa Ahsan were not part of the Pakistan U-19 side that defeated England 3-1 in a four-match Youth ODI series in September.

Pakistan won the previous edition of the tournament in the United Arab Emirates, defeating arch-rivals India by 191 runs in a one-sided final at the ICC Academy Ground in Dubai.

The team will begin their title defence against the UAE on Nov 6 before taking on India on Nov 8 and Nepal on Nov 10.

Group ‘B’ comprises Afghanistan, Bangladesh, Sri Lanka and Malaysia.

The semi-finals will be played on Nov 12, with the final scheduled for Nov 14.

Shahid Anwar will serve as head coach and team manager, while Rao Iftikhar Anjum has been named fast bowling coach and Zohaib Khan spin bowling coach. Humayun Farhat will be the fielding coach.

item.title: An opportunity to build industrial capacity. [ dhakatribune ]
item.description:
Bangladesh’s medical device market represents a significant economic opportunity that still remains largely untapped. As demand for healthcare grows, the country continues to depend heavily on imported equipment and supplies, leaving a potentially valuable domestic industry underdeveloped.
This needs to change -- not only to reduce import dependence, but also to strengthen our healthcare system and create new avenues for investment and employment.
While developing a domestic medical device industry will require considerable investment, technical expertise, quality control, and strict adherence to international standards, these challenges should encourage us to develop the necessary capacity rather than remain content with importing products that could eventually be manufactured at home.
The first step must, therefore, be creating a supportive environment for local manufacturers. Access to affordable financing, tax incentives for genuine investment, reliable infrastructure, and streamlined regulatory procedures can encourage businesses to enter the sector. Partnerships between local entrepreneurs, universities, research institutions, and international manufacturers can also facilitate technology transfer and help develop a skilled workforce.
Quality must remain central to this effort: Medical devices directly affect patient safety, and domestic production cannot be allowed to become an excuse to compromise with our standards.
Strong regulatory oversight, transparent certification procedures and investment in research and development will be essential to building confidence among healthcare providers and patients.
Additionally, where locally manufactured products meet the necessary quality and performance requirements, government hospitals could be encouraged to consider them, giving domestic businesses a dependable market in which to grow.
Such support, however, must promote genuine competitiveness rather than protect inefficient producers indefinitely.
Ultimately, our growing healthcare needs should be seen as an opportunity to build industrial capacity. Reducing import dependence will certainly take time, sustained investment, and consistent policies, but with the right support, Bangladesh can turn an overlooked market into a source of economic growth, skilled employment, and greater healthcare security.

item.description:
Muneeba Ali will captain Pakistan in the ICC Women’s Emerging Nations Trophy 2026, with the Pakistan Cricket Board (PCB) on Tuesday announcing a 14-member squad for the tournament to be held in Ajman, United Arab Emirates, from Nov 12 to 25.

Batter Ayesha Zafar has been appointed vice-captain of the side, which will feature 12 players retained from Pakistan’s previous assignment. Sadaf Shamas and Waheeda Akhtar have been recalled to the squad.

Regular captain Fatima Sana will miss the tournament as she prepares to feature in her maiden Women’s Big Bash League season in Australia.

The squad announcement comes after Pakistan secured a bronze medal at the Asian Games in Japan. Wicket-keeper-batter Gull Feroza, who was named the best wicketkeeper-batter at the recently concluded National Women’s T20 Tournament, has also been included.

The batting line-up comprises Ayesha, Eman Naseer, Eyman Fatima, Sadaf, Saira Jabeen and Shawaal Zulfiqar, while Muneeba and Gull provide wicket-keeping options.

Left-arm spinner Nashra Sundhu will spearhead the bowling attack, with Momina Riasat, Tuba Hassan and Umm-e-Hani completing the spin contingent. Tasmia Rubab and Waheeda are the two frontline pace options.

The 30-match tournament will feature 10 teams divided into two groups. Pakistan have been placed in Group B alongside Bangladesh, Thailand, the Netherlands and Zimbabwe.

Group ‘A’ comprises Sri Lanka, Ireland, Scotland, Papua New Guinea and hosts the United Arab Emirates.

The teams will first compete in a single-league round-robin stage, after which the top three sides from each group will advance to the Super Six stage. Each qualifying team will play three matches in that phase, with the top two progressing to the final on Nov 25.

The Pakistan squad will assemble in Lahore on Nov 6 and attend a pre-tournament training camp on Nov 7, 8 and 9 before departing for the UAE.
